title: What's the Pygmalion Effect?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Pygmalion effect, a self-fulfilling prophecy in which high expectations from teachers, managers, or others lead people to perform better. They trace the term to Robert Merton (1948) and the Ovid Pygmalion story, then cover Rosenthal and Jacobson's 1963 "maze bright" rat experiment and their 1968 Oak School study and book "Pygmalion in the Classroom," including its statistical flaws (the made-up Harvard Test of Inflected Acquisition, the misused Togo test, missing raw data, cherry-picked results). They discuss the media reaction, the academic debate, the 1978 Rosenthal and Donald Rubin meta-analysis, business and military applications, and teacher strategies such as warm climate, challenging work, detailed feedback, and mixed-ability grouping. They also cover the Golem and Galatea effects and Christine Rubie-Davies's Teacher Expectation Project. The episode closes with a listener mail from Steve of Chapter/Charter Books in Rhode Island about New York Times bestseller list reporting.

segments.title: Opening and Pygmalion myth
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Pygmalion effect as a self-fulfilling prophecy and expectancy bias, and the hosts recall the Ovid and Shaw/My Fair Lady versions of the Pygmalion story.

segments.title: Origins of the term and the rat study
segments.summary: The term self-fulfilling prophecy is credited to Robert Merton in 1948. In 1963 Rosenthal and Kermit Fode ran a maze experiment with rats labeled maze bright or maze dull, though the rats were randomly assigned.

segments.title: Rosenthal, Jacobson, and the Oak School
segments.summary: Principal Leonore Jacobson offered her San Francisco school for a study, and Rosenthal took her up on it. The school grouped students by reading ability.

segments.title: The bloomer experiment design and results
segments.summary: Teachers were told some students were bloomers based on a fake test, the Test of Inflected Acquisition, which was actually an IQ test called the Togo test. Younger bloomers gained IQ points over two years, while older grades showed no such gains.

segments.title: Explanations and the 1968 book
segments.summary: Rosenthal explained the younger-grade results by malleability and teacher attention. The 1968 study was published as a paper and a book, Pygmalion in the Classroom, which drew heavy press coverage.

segments.title: Press hype versus academic critique
segments.summary: The book was promoted in the press as proof, while the book omitted results that did not fit, such as negative correlations in older grades. Josh notes Rosenthal did not push back on the simplified coverage.

segments.title: Academic criticism of the methodology
segments.summary: Critics noted the Togo test was not meant for young children or IQs under 60, that raw data was not published, that teachers gave the tests, and that teachers did not remember the bloomer lists. Rosenthal defended the results by saying the same test over time still showed gains.

segments.title: Scale analogy and critiques continued
segments.summary: Chuck uses a broken scale analogy to explain why the gains were not meaningful, and Josh adds that the original results were skewed. Richard Snow and others are referenced.

segments.title: Debate, replication, and vindication
segments.summary: Robert Snow suggested the study might have accidentally found a real effect. Over a decade of debate, better studies supported the Pygmalion effect's existence to some degree.

segments.title: Political readings and ability tracking
segments.summary: Different camps read the findings differently: a San Francisco Chronicle writer blamed teacher expectations, while Albert Shanker blamed poverty and class sizes. Josh discusses pushes to end AP and remedial tracks.

segments.title: Meta-analysis and workplace studies
segments.summary: In 1978 Rosenthal and Donald Rubin analyzed 345 studies. Effects were strongest in military and business settings, including a medical kit assembly group whose productivity rose after managers were told they were promising.

segments.title: Teacher strategies: climate, feedback, and tasks
segments.summary: Chuck outlines four areas teachers can use to convey positive expectations: a warm emotional climate, more challenging assignments, more chances to engage with material, and more detailed feedback.

segments.title: Uneven attention and patronizing low performers
segments.summary: Teachers who focused attention on low-performing students did not always close the gap; Rhona Weinstein suggested students sensed low expectations. Hosts discuss labeling and separating students.

segments.title: Christine Rubie-Davies and the Teacher Expectation Project
segments.summary: Rubie-Davies's project trains teachers to hold high expectations for all students without deception. Key ideas include knowing all students equally well, mixed-ability groups, respectful language, and student-set goals.

segments.title: Praising effort and personal anecdotes
segments.summary: Rubie-Davies's advice includes praising effort over accuracy and treating students equally. Chuck describes being well liked by teachers as a class clown.

segments.title: Golem and Galatea effects
segments.summary: The hosts define the Golem effect as the negative counterpart of low expectations and the Galatea effect as self-expectations that shape performance through authority figures' views.

segments.title: Listener mail from Steve of Charter Books
segments.summary: Steve, a Rhode Island bookseller, confirms how the New York Times bestseller list gets its sales data and describes bulk-order inquiries and book laundering. Josh encourages supporting indie bookstores.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives the email address for listener mail and signs off.
